html:
In 2005 Kazakhstan finished the Kokaral Dam, a 12-kilometre dike that split the small northern part of the Aral Sea from the dying southern part. With help from the World Bank, it brought the North Aral Sea back to life.

Since the 1960s Soviet irrigation had starved the sea, and by the 1980s it had broken in two (Aral Sea begins to shrink). The northern part is fed by the Syr Darya. Earlier sand dikes had washed out. The concrete and earth dam now keeps the river's water in the north instead of letting it flow away into the south.

The North Aral rose faster than expected, its water became less salty, and native fish such as pike-perch came back. Fishing boats returned and fish processing restarted, bringing jobs back to towns such as Aralsk, though the shore is still far from the old harbour. The price was the fate of the south: the larger South Aral, mostly in Uzbekistan, kept shrinking.
sum: In 2005 Kazakhstan finished the Kokaral Dam, a 12-kilometre dike that split the small northern part of the Aral Sea from the dying southern part. With help from the World Bank, it brought the North Aral Sea back to life.
